items.description: A sealed glass vial of mushroom spores. The one crop that asks almost nothing of you — a little damp, a little dark, and it will grow where nothing else will.
A knuckle of pale root, wrapped in damp cloth. Plant it deep and wait. It will not thank you for hurrying.
A hard, soot-dark seed head salvaged from a field that never stopped burning. It grows fast and greedy — and it drinks clean water like it remembers the rain.
A folded paper of golden grain, labelled in a careful hand. From before. From when a field was just a field.
A lead-lined tray of sifted earth, deep enough for roots. One plot, one chance. Stack them against the dark.
A salvaged horticultural lamp, jury-rigged to a car battery. It throws a thin, hungry light — enough to convince a seed that the sun still exists.
A heavy sheet of leaded glass. It turns the killing light into something a leaf can bear — and keeps the falling ash out of the soil. Cracks easily.
A bitter copper-sulfate wash in a dented tin. It will not save a crop that has already gone black — but it can stop one from getting there.
A brick of sterilised substrate — clean earth, scrubbed of the worst of what is out there. Lays down a kinder bed for a seed than the floor of a bunker.
Pale caps grown in the damp dark of the planter box. Not much, but they grew. That still means something.
A small, dense root, boiled soft. Sticks to the ribs and to the memory of anyone who can remember what a meal used to be.
A handful of soot-dark grain, threshed and winnowed by hand. Rough bread. Real bread, all the same.
Golden grain, the colour of a field no one alive has seen. Ground to flour, it makes bread that tastes the way the old songs said it did. People weep over it, quietly, and do not say why.
Food grown in soil that remembers the ash, or spoiled in the damp. It fills the belly. It also remembers the ash.
A forged steel hand trowel with a turned wooden handle. Indispensable for working tight planter flats and setting delicate rootings.
Short bypass shears with carbon-steel blades and a wire latch. Clean cuts prevent stem rot and preserve growing vines.
A seam-soldered tin-plate watering can with a perforated brass rose. Delivers gentle irrigation without washing away topsoil.
A three-pronged steel claw for breaking up soil crust and raking out root tangles between dense greenhouse rows.
Rich, dark organic humus sifted from aerated decay bins. Replenishes depleted nitrogen and restores soil structure.
Fine, grey hardwood ash rich in potassium and carbonate. Sweetens sour, acidic soils and bolsters stalk rigidity.
A foul-smelling liquid concentrate brewed from hydrolyzed fish scrap. Highly concentrated nutrition for fast vegetative growth.
Potassium fatty-acid concentrate that suffocates mites, thrips, and aphids without poisoning edible foliage.
Bright yellow adhesive cards hung above crop canopies. Intercepts flying insect pests and monitors infestation pressure.
Fine woven nylon barrier netting for greenhouse vents and planter hoods. Stops burrowing and crawling pests physically.
Coiled micro-tubing, barbed emitter stakes, and junction tees. Channels metered water directly to roots with minimal evaporative loss.
An inline stainless-mesh cartridge that strains fine sediment and algae flakes before they foul micro-irrigation emitters.
A heavy reinforced vinyl membrane with drain grommets and collector brackets for channeling condensation and runoff.
A clear tempered glass pane salvaged from an agricultural bay. Replaces shattered roof panels to admit full spectrum light.
Tough, treated polyethylene film designed to withstand continuous ultraviolet exposure without yellowing or brittle failure.
Knitted agricultural netting that blocks scorching solar radiation and cuts heat stress across sensitive seedling beds.
